By Steve Holland and Ryan Patrick Jones
WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which will begin next Thursday, the White House said on Friday.
The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defence Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on Tuesday to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," a White House statement said.
Ukraine's top negotiator, David Arakhamia, said on Telegram that the humanitarian operation would start once a ceasefire was in place.
He said the accord, the result of a long process involving Melania Trump and Pope Leo, would set up a humanitarian corridor for residents to leave and allow assistance into the town.
In Moscow, the Kremlin welcomed the agreement. It praised Melania Trump's role in securing the agreement and said President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin had discussed details.
The Kremlin said earlier this week that work was under way to ease the humanitarian situation in Oleshky after Putin told the pope he was ready to cooperate on the issue.
The development comes as President Trump pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to reach an agreement with Putin to end the war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
FIRST LADY HAS SOUGHT TO HELP UKRAINIAN CHILDREN
Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," Melania Trump said in the statement.
The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from both countries to visit residents in their homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed American media organization accompanying the teams to document the process, the first lady said.
Newsmax, a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted "exclusive access to document the effort."
Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people — primarily elderly residents, along with about 50 children — down from roughly 24,000 before the war, the White House said. About 90% of the city was flooded following the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House.
The statement said Melania Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
(Reporting by Steve Holland and Susan Heavey; Writing by Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto; Editing by Katharine Jackson, David Ljunggren, Caitlin Webber, Rod Nickel and Ron Popeski)

articles.title: The Existential Crisis Of Statehood: Proliferation And Operational Impacts Of Proxy Warfare In Middle Eastern Conflicts - Analysis - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: The Existential Crisis Of Statehood: Proliferation And Operational Impacts Of Proxy Warfare In Middle Eastern Conflicts - Analysis  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- Erosion of the Weberian Monopoly on Physical Violence: Modern proxy warfare is counterintuitive to historical processes of state-building, with arming, financing, and training sub-state actors beyond constitutional structures, creating a destabilizing ‘oligopoly of violence’.
- Institutional Infiltration and Hybrid Sovereignty: Iranian-backed proxy networks use the weakness of the state within the region to create parallel political, military, and economic systems; they receive public funding and enjoy state immunity and constitutional impunity and are not subject to civilian oversight.
- Shift from Pan-Arabism to Statist Preservation (Wataniyya): There has been a significant paradigm shift in the political agendas of the region from the 20th-century concept of trans-state Arab unity (Qawmiyya) to the need to protect territorial sovereignty, state borders, and nation-state existence (Wataniyya).
- Great Power Disruption and Transactional Failure: Superpowers and global competitors—such as the United States, Russia, and China—use the Middle East as a zero-sum space of influence, prioritizing short-term counterterrorism, energy security, or geopolitical leverage over supporting the strengthening of Middle East state authority.
Introduction
The nation-state has been the most contested and least taken-for-granted political form in the modern Middle East. The territorial map of the region, largely laid out during the imperial reordering of the post-World War I era, has remained cartographically persistent. Still, the internal substance of state sovereignty in the region has been increasingly eroded. Following the Arab Uprisings of 2011, it was widely predicted that the borders drawn by Sykes-Picot were destined to disappear due to the free movement of people or sub-state fragmentation, but this never came to pass. Practical administrative powers of the States wielded within these borders, however, have greatly eroded, and the gap between de facto administrative control and domestic legitimacy, and de jure legal sovereignty (international recognition), has significantly widened.
Post-colonial independence produced many ‘hard, weak states’ that were structurally fragile and institutionally lacking strong civic legitimacy, yet coercively authoritarian in their behavior towards domestic dissent. The random delineation of imperial borders created a degree of incongruity between the borders and identities, sowing seeds of irredentism and structural vulnerabilities in the regional system. The struggle of sub-state or trans-state identity networks thus remained a continual threat to modern statehood in the Middle East, while the domestic state’s concerns centered on the regime’s survival.
The current status of the Middle Eastern nation-state can only be understood by studying the state’s internal structural weaknesses and the external actors that exploit it. Certain of these external dynamics are the most acrimonious challenges to statehood in the region today, above all the constant proliferation of asymmetric proxy warfare. Proxy war is an active erosion of the state that undermines the monopoly on physical violence, institutionalizes hybrid forms of government, and involves non-state armed actors in the host state’s constitutional and administrative power structure. Modern proxy war is not a war to overthrow the international boundary; it is a war that undermines the central state from within by exploiting structural differences at home. External sponsors arm sub-state proxies with high kinetic power and turn states into places of constant security rivalry, endangering the very survival of Westphalian governance in the Middle East.
From Pan-Arab Unification to Statist Preservation: The Reordering of Regional Priorities
Throughout the twentieth century, there was a strong push for supranational ideational movements to question the legitimacy of individual states in the Middle East. Arab nationalism was an anti-colonial movement that stood for nationhood, asserting that all Arabic-speaking peoples were a single, undivided nation (al-Umma al-‘Arabiyya) united by language, history, culture, and a sense of collective identity. It began in the late nineteenth century, during the so-called Nahda (Arab Awakening) under Ottoman rule. After the First World War and the establishment of the Western mandate regimes, the Arab nationalist movement became a fervent anti-imperialist movement that demanded political unification of the Arab community under the slogan of pan-Arabism (Qawmiyya).
In Pan-Arabism, post-colonial territories were viewed as artificial, temporary, and divisive constructs of European colonial powers. Classical Pan-Arab ideologues asserted that the Arab world was divided into independent states, a historical aberration that could not stand and had to be rectified by achieving pan-Arab unity. In this ideology, it was considered that the security and interests of the whole Arab nation (raison de la nation Arabe) were of absolute moral value and priority over the narrow self-interest of any state (raison d’état). The notion of individual state sovereignty (Wataniyya) was often denounced by Pan-Arabists as “regionalism” or disloyalty to the anti-imperialist cause.
The zenith of Pan-Arabism was during the 1950s and 1960s when the charismatic Egyptian President, Gamal Abdel Nasser, led the way. In 1956, Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal, and in his victory over the British, French, and Israeli forces, Cairo came to wield great trans-state ideological influence. Nasser appealed directly to the populations of neighboring Arab states via Radio Cairo’s Sawt al-Arab and played on popular pressure within the country against pro-Western conservative regimes. To a large degree, Nasser created an informal norm of regional behavior that established standards of conduct, thereby limiting the sovereignty of individual states and punishing states seeking security alliances outside regional “collective” security systems.
The most explicit effort to realize the Pan-Arab dream was in February 1958 when Nasser unified Egypt and Syria into the United Arab Republic (UAR). The UAR was a policy of political incorporation, in which the state sovereignty of each member state was supposed to disappear in favor of a single regional state. The UAR experiment, however, very quickly revealed the fundamental conflict between unionist ideals and structural realities. The union was highly centralized in Cairo, with the Egyptian military and technocrats controlling key offices; the Syrian political parties were disorganized, and Egyptian economic policies were imposed on Syria. The union was not an equal one for the political and military elites of Syria, who felt frustrated by their subservient position to Egypt, and saw it as a form of Egyptian administrative rule that looked to promote the Egyptian state rather than unity. In September 1961, the Damascus military coup dissolved the UAR and reestablished Syria’s independent statehood. The UAR’s demise dealt a major blow to the cause of Pan-Arabism, as it became clear that even ideologically similar peoples were unwilling to give up their local statehood and administrative autonomy.
While the UAR revealed the structural weaknesses of pan-Arab unification, the catastrophic Arab defeat in the Six-Day War of June 1967 brought an end to the pan-Arab ideology. The rapid military collapse of the Arabs undermined the revolutionary regimes’ most important claims to regional leadership and anti-imperialist legitimacy. Following 1967, Arab foreign policy made a turning point: a fundamental change in emphasis from the ideational to the pragmatic dimension and from trans-state action to Westphalian statecraft. Self-help, territorial defense, and realpolitik power balancing were the sole means of survival adopted by Arab regimes in response to the serious security threats they faced. Internal state-building was further encouraged by the regularities of war and increased domestic revenue flows from the 1970s oil boom, leading to greater state strength and resistance to external ideological subversion by individual governments. The notion of patriotism and loyalty based on the individual territorial state, called Wataniyya, became the dominant factor in international relations in the Middle East, replacing Qawmiyya.
The contemporary political leaders play the role of Arab nationalists (neo-pan-Arabism) defensively, not with the intent of creating a unified entity that would diminish the importance of the state and increase the power of the pan-Arab movement. The politics of the region is less about seeking to “blur boundaries” than about a fierce, defensive effort to preserve and strengthen the state. The modern regional order in the Middle East is focused on the security of state structures, national boundaries, and the integrity against sub-state disintegration. Unlike in the mid-twentieth century, when states embraced the option of political merger, today’s governments in the Middle East are driven to preserve the nation-state and its security against armed sub-state actors and other proxy forces that aim to weaken the state from within.
De-Structuring the Sovereign State: Iranian Proxy Networks and Great Power Dynamics
Non-state armed actors within asymmetric proxy networks pose the greatest current threat to state survival in the Middle East. This is the approach that the Islamic Republic of Iran has followed, building an advanced regional network dubbed the “Axis of Resistance” (Mihwar al-Muqawama). Iran’s proxy model was launched in the wake of the Islamic Revolution in 1979 and is being managed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps – Quds Force (IRGC-QF), giving Tehran the ability to deploy asymmetric force, create strategic depth, and intimidate regional and global opponents, without facing the financial burden or the direct military threat of conventional interstate conflict.

articles.summary: Russia strikes Kyiv with three cluster-warhead ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy says  Euronews.comRussia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine  The GuardianRussia bombards Ukraine after Trump envoy hails ‘humanitarian’ Putin  The TimesRussia and Ukraine trade fresh strikes despite renewed push for U.S.-brokered peace talks  CNBCRussia bombs Kyiv and Ukraine fires drones towards Moscow, despite talk of renewing negotiati...
articles.full_text:
The latest Russian bombardment of Ukraine's capital came just hours after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, underscoring the stark contrast between Washington's renewed diplomatic efforts and Moscow's continuing attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight with three ballistic missiles carrying cluster warheads designed to inflict maximum casualties across densely populated areas, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Thursday.
One of the missiles struck Pechersk, the Ukrainian capital's historic centre, hitting an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery, damaging religious buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.
The missiles were designed to detonate in the air as they approached their targets, dispersing explosive submunitions across an area 400 metres in diameter, Zelenskyy said.
Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukraine's presidential adviser known by his callsign "Flash", earlier identified one of the missiles as an Iskander equipped with a K5 cluster warhead.
At least two dead and dozens injured
"This warhead detonates above the ground and is used specifically for inflicting maximum harm to people and equipment over an area of 400 by 400 metres," Beskrestnov said, adding that its 58 bomblets explode in the air.
Zelenskyy accused Moscow of deliberately targeting civilians in Kyiv's historic centre, insisting that the choice of both weapon and location was intentional.
"This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing because it was no accident. The choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible," he said.
"There was no military target nearby, not even in theory, and the weapon was designed to cause widespread destruction."
The strike was part of a large-scale Russian aerial assault on the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region overnight on 21–22 October.
At least two people were killed and 34 others injured, including five children, across the affected areas, according to Zelenskyy.
The bombardment came in several waves, with ballistic missiles and drones striking residential neighbourhoods, transport facilities and medical infrastructure across the capital.
Kyiv authorities reported damage in the Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Dniprovskyi districts.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 210 drones, including 110 jet-powered variants, alongside Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon and Onyx missiles.
Ukrainian air defences intercepted or suppressed 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered variants, while strikes were recorded at 32 locations and falling debris at another eight.
Zelenskyy said Russia had fired 21 missiles in total during three waves of ballistic strikes on Kyiv.
The attacks continued throughout Thursday, with further strikes reported in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Marhanets, Mykolaiv and Kherson, as well as several other regions. In Kharkiv, a commuter train was hit, according to the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out more than 170 strikes against critical energy facilities since 11 October, despite Ukrainian air defences intercepting significant numbers of drones and some missiles.
He warned that Ukrainian intelligence identified Russian priorities for further attacks in the coming weeks, accusing Moscow of exploiting delays in Western air defence supplies.
"Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defence supplies from our partners," he said, calling for the accelerated delivery of military assistance already approved by Ukraine's allies.
The overnight bombardment came just hours after US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg as Washington sought to revive negotiations to end the war.
During the visit, Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian", despite the Russian president being wanted by the International Criminal Court over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that Ukraine was ready to accept literally any form of truce, on any aspect of the war, that Russia would be willing to agree to.
But following the latest attacks, the Ukrainian president questioned Moscow's willingness to pursue peace.
"Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it," he said.

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a temporary ceasefire around the besieged town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, the White House said on Friday.
The localised ceasefire will allow humanitarian aid to enter the town and for civilians to be evacuated, according to a statement from the office of Melania Trump, the First Lady, who helped to secure the deal along with Pope Leo XIV.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” the first lady said. “Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water.”
Pope Leo spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin last Friday to appeal for a humanitarian ceasefire while the Chicago-born Catholic spiritual leader was in hospital in Rome recovering from an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, according to a Vatican statement.
The ceasefire was confirmed by one of Ukraine’s chief negotiators, David Arakhamia, in a post on social media, in which he thanked the Pope and the first lady for their role in brokering the deal. Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the ceasefire would guarantee “the free movement of civilians from Oleshky”.
Dmitry Peskov, Putin’s spokesperson, said Russia’s military was working on timing for a ceasefire in Oleshky.
He described setting up the corridor as “a large and complex operation” but declined to go into details about how it would work or how long it would last.
Peskov said Moscow did not have “rose-tinted glasses” about the initiative because Ukraine had not agreed to stop its attacks on Russian territory and continued to receive US military assistance, according to Tass.
Previous attempts to carry out limited ceasefires between Russia and Ukraine for humanitarian purposes have been marred by accusations of widespread violations.
Donald Trump’s recently announced energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv collapsed as the Kremlin continued to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and kill civilians.
Oleshky, which had a prewar population of 24,000 and has been under occupation since 2022, sits across the Dnipro River from the regional capital of Kherson.
Roads around the city are heavily mined and drones are a near-constant presence in the skies, which have made it dangerous to evacuate or bring in food and fuel.
The last food delivery to the city was in May and there are reports of local residents eating grass to survive, Ukrainian human rights defender and Nobel laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk said earlier this week.
Local residents have struggled to bury those who have died owing to the threat posed by Russian drones, she said.
Ukrainian forces have resorted to airlifting food into the city by drone in an attempt to ease the humanitarian crisis for residents trapped in the city.

articles.title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran - The Guardian
articles.summary: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran  The GuardianIstanbul meeting: A new division of labor in the Iran war?  Iran InternationalEuropean, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks  Al JazeeraTurkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way  ReutersEgypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan say 'Israeli occupation main source of regional instability'  The Times of Israel
articles.full_text:
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

articles.title: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war - AP News
articles.summary: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war  AP NewsShip attacks in Strait of Hormuz hit record high in October  ReutersIran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response  Al JazeeraIran says 7 vessels hit near Strait of Hormuz, warns US of wider response  NewsNationStrait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says  Fox News
articles.full_text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
“Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.
He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.
Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.”
Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region
Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.
The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.
October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.
Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.
Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks
Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence.
Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.
Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday.
The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped return oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.
UN urges US and Iran to return to diplomacy to end conflict, reopen strait
U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said no commercial ships should be attacked and called for diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran to reopen the strait.
“For the sake of the people of the region and for the broader world, we need to see that waterway reopen, and we need to see tensions go down,” he told reporters Thursday.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.
Iran has warned that it learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, indicating in recent days that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.
The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.
Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.
Iran still promotes its latest proposal to end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions, including ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. It echoes conditions in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected the latest proposal last month, but both sides acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.
The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes
A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.
The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency.
Now the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.
The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.
The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.
Meanwhile, the president of Saudi oil company Aramco, whose sites have been targeted by the Houthis, said the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has increased threefold in light of the global energy crisis.
The East-West pipeline’s capacity has surged from two million to seven million barrels each day, Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business. He said the company has been using drones to assess any damage to the pipeline and help with firefighting.

articles.title: General Zubair Mahmood Hayat Warns of More Dangerous Pakistan, India Crises Without Conflict Resolution - ProPakistani
articles.summary: General Zubair Mahmood Hayat Warns of More Dangerous Pakistan, India Crises Without Conflict Resolution  ProPakistani
articles.full_text:
Former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee Gen. Zubair Mahmood Hayat on Wednesday stressed the need to resolve the underlying disputes between Pakistan and India, warning that ending a crisis without addressing its root causes only sets the stage for a more dangerous confrontation.
“Terminating a crisis without addressing its root causes only sets the stage for the next, more dangerous conflict,” Gen Zubair said at the concluding session of the second Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference, hosted by the Strategic Vision Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank specializing in strategic issues.
“In the subcontinent, the core issue of Jammu of Kashmir cannot be wished away, or scrutinized out of existence, or reduced to an administrative matter. Similarly, water cannot be converted from a shared necessity into an instrument of power and pressure,” he maintained while stressing resolution of Kashmir dispute and restoration of Indus Water Treaty.
Gen Zubair warned that repeated crises between the nuclear armed neighbors could become increasingly dangerous if unresolved disputes, diminishing restraint and the absence of sustained political dialogue continued to undermine regional security.
“Where disputes remain unresolved and restraint became a diminishing asset, each successfully terminated crisis can tempt a revisionist actor, like India, to begin the next one higher on the ladder,” he said.
Referring to the May 2025 military conflict between Pakistan and India, Gen Zubair said Pakistan demonstrated its military capabilities and political control through a calibrated response that prevented India from imposing a unilateral fait accompli without triggering an unlimited war.
The conflict, he said, underscored the limits of relying on deterrence alone to prevent future confrontations.
“The larger lesson is not that conflict between two nuclear armed neighbors can be made routine; it is that there is no tested and certified safe space for war,” he said.
Gen Zubair warned that any future crisis could unfold under different circumstances, involving new technologies, different political leaders and significantly compressed decision making timelines, increasing the risk of miscalculation and unintended escalation.
He said South Asia remained short of lasting peace because it lacked an inclusive regional security framework, effective crisis management mechanisms and sustained political dialogue. He attributed the situation to India’s Hindutva ideology and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS.
“The region lives between deterrence that prevents the worst and disputes that repeatedly regenerate danger,” he said.
He also warned that unverified allegations could trigger a major conflict before governments had established the facts. He, therefore, warned that a future conflict could begin through an accident rather than a deliberate decision by a state, particularly when allegations spread faster than they can be verified. He cited the continuing Operation Sindhoor in this context.
SVI Executive Director Dr Naeem Salik speaking at one of the working sessions said the weakening of the international arms control architecture, growing uncertainty surrounding extended nuclear deterrence, and intensifying strategic competition among major powers are increasing global nuclear risks.
The absence of effective restraints on strategic nuclear arsenals, he maintained, underscores the urgent need to reinvigorate arms control, strategic dialogue, and international confidence building measures.
The integration of artificial intelligence, cyber capabilities, and advanced conventional weapons into military operations, he feared, was creating new pathways to nuclear escalation.
“The growing entanglement of conventional and nuclear command and control systems, early warning infrastructure, and strategic assets increases the risks of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and premature nuclear decision-making,” Dr Salik asserted.
The two day Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference brought together Pakistani and international nuclear experts to discuss regional deterrence, lessons from the May 2025 conflict, the changing global nuclear order and options for reducing nuclear risks. Its agenda also covered the erosion of arms control frameworks, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and hypersonic weapons, the militarization of space, ballistic missile defense and the implications of great-power competition for global non-proliferation efforts.

Reporting on cyberattacks against Japanese entities rose 48% between Q2 and Q3 2026, encompassing ransomware, exploitation of vulnerabilities, credential leaks, and service disruptions. Significant incidents exposed millions of customer records and disrupted operations across multiple sectors, with attacks on shared service providers extending the impact to downstream organizations. Further incidents in October 2026 indicate that these trends have persisted into Q4. This report examines potential contributing factors, including demand for Japanese personal information, legacy systems, software vulnerabilities, weak API controls, and AI’s likely role in lowering technical and language barriers. New incident-reporting requirements under Japan’s Active Cyber Defense (ACD) law, effective October 1, may further increase the number of disclosures of incidents affecting Japanese organizations.
At least two features set the Q3 Japan breaches apart from other such breaches. The first is the breadth of the attacks: victim organizations spanned the retail, rail, logistics, media, education, and software industries, and the intrusions involved ransomware, stolen cloud credentials, and exploited web-facing systems. The second is the scale of the attacks: single incidents now routinely affect millions of user records or organizations downstream that rely on the targeted services, such as roughly 33 million records leaked from the EPARK PeakManager reservation platform in July and 6.6 million accounts from Times Car in September.
This trend has continued into Q4. On October 7, a ransomware incident affected IDCFrontier, a Japanese cloud provider, disrupting 495 companies and local governments. Almost a week later, on October 13, 2026, a data breach affected the Japanese software company Sourcenext. In this incident, an unidentified third party misused the company’s member information retrieval API to compromise 22,519,960 customer records containing personally identifiable information, including email addresses, passwords, names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employment information, and more.
Our observations complement October 2026 warnings issued by several Japanese agencies, including the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center (JPCERT/CC), the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), and the Innovation Platform Agency (IPA), regarding a series of cyberattacks targeting Japan-based organizations. JPCERT/CC’s notice warned of at least four consistent tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) linked to recent incidents:
- Exploitation of known vulnerabilities in unpatched systems or misconfigurations;
- Attacking internal and external APIs, sometimes using stolen API credentials;
- Exploitation of CVE-2026-72898 (CVSS score 10), a SQL injection vulnerability, in the Metabase application;
- The deployment of web shells contained within .war and .jsp files on internet-accessible web servers.
Later reports attributed the cyberattacks targeting Japanese company websites to artificial intelligence (AI) agents linked to activity ranging from basic website scanning to extended attack sequences that involved multiple tools and techniques.
Japan-based Macnica Security also reported a surge in cyberattacks since July 2026 involving personal information leaks from web systems. The company noted that this increase is unique to Japan compared with other countries. According to Macnica, of the 119 cases disclosed in 2026, approximately 68% were announced since July. This accounts for about 31% of the total 265 cases over a 34-month period. The company similarly observed unauthorized access through weak authentication, stolen credentials, or exploited software vulnerabilities and site-specific flaws in application design, APIs, or access controls. Macnica could not confirm the use of AI in these attacks.
Explaining the Increase in Incidents
Multiple factors are likely responsible for the recent increase in attacks affecting Japanese organizations.
- High Demand in the Criminal Ecosystem for Japanese User Data: Criminals on the dark web place a premium on data from Japanese organizations due to Japan’s financial and identification requirements and its status as a wealthy, developed economy.
- Widespread Use of Legacy Systems and Software: According to an April 2026 article by Money Forward, more than 60% of Japanese firms still use legacy systems, end-of-life software, and older operating systems. Such systems no longer receive security updates and official patches from vendors, leaving known flaws exposed to increasingly automated attempts to exploit them.
- Operationalization of AI Tooling: While the specific models abused are not yet confirmed, commercial AI products are widely believed to have been leveraged in the recent spate of attacks against Japanese organizations, both for automating the attack sequence (such as automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation), and for reducing the barrier-to-entry historically attributed to the complexity of the Japanese language (such as through the easier drafting of convincing phishing emails in proper business Japanese). Notably, financial institutions in neighboring South Korea were recently the target of an intrusion campaign leveraging ARTEX, a Chinese open-source AI penetration-testing tool attributed to a group Recorded Future refers to as TAG-217. On October 19, the Japanese cybersecurity company GMO Cybersecurity by Ierae reportedly concluded that ARTEX was used in attacks against roughly 80 Japanese companies, with 8 of those attacks occurring in the 30 days prior to its report.
- New Incident Reporting Requirements: Effective October 1, 2026, Japan’s new Active Cyber Defense (ACD) Law imposes mandatory reporting requirements on designated critical infrastructure operators. This is unlikely to account for the surge in reported incidents due to the law’s implementation date in Q4 2026, but it does imply that we will very likely continue to observe a higher volume of incident disclosures from Japanese organizations going forward, and the impending implementation of the law may have induced some organizations to disclose incidents in Q3 that would otherwise have gone unreported.
Recommendations
Insikt Group recommends that Japanese organizations consider the following:
- Migrate away from and/or update legacy systems. Outdated and unpatched devices or software (including operating systems) provide an attractive, easy vector for threat actors to compromise organizations via previously disclosed vulnerabilities and exploits. AI-enabled scanning and automated exploitation have further increased the risk to these systems. Where possible, replace end-of-life hardware and software.
- Harden internet-facing systems. Secure internet-exposed hardware and services such as virtual private network (VPN) servers, web application firewalls, load balancers, small office/home office routers, IP cameras, and DVRs by patching known vulnerabilities, restricting administrative access, enabling additional logging, and disabling unnecessary services. These devices have been increasingly exploited by cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors alike over the last several years for initial access.
- Strengthen API controls. Verify authorization for every API request, test whether users can access other customers’ records, restrict API key privileges, and limit bulk data retrieval.
- Protect accounts against phishing. Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) and train staff to be vigilant against increasingly well-crafted Japanese-language phishing messages.
- Limit data exposure and prepare for disruption. Delete unnecessary personal information, restrict data export permissions, test restoration from protected backups, and establish manual alternatives for critical services such as reservations and dispatch.
- Adopt privileged access management (PAM). Limit administrative and super-user accounts, providing elevated rights only on a temporary, just-in-time basis.
- Use Recorded Future Threat Intelligence. Customers can proactively monitor for threat actor mentions of their organization and leaked data on dark web forums, chat rooms, and ransomware leak sites by configuring alerts on the Recorded Future Intelligence Platform, regularly ingesting Insikt Group research, and blocklisting known malicious indicators of compromise (IoCs).
Chinese Guarantee Marketplaces
How do Chinese-language guarantee marketplaces support fraud campaigns targeting Japan? Explore Insikt Group’s guarantee marketplace reports to understand how these ecosystems connect criminal groups and facilitate scams, phishing campaigns, and the trade in stolen personal information.
Insikt Group adheres to responsible disclosure procedures in conducting its research.

articles.title: War At Sea: The Maritime Crisis And The Forgotten Rights Of Seafarers – Analysis - Eurasia Review

Key Takeaways:
- Escalating conflicts—from Russia’s war in Ukraine disrupting Black Sea grain shipments, to Houthi attacks forcing diversions around the Cape of Good Hope, to the post-28 February 2026 US-Israel-Iran confrontation—have turned major maritime routes including the Strait of Hormuz into conflict zones, trapping approximately 6,000 seafarers and causing deaths, vessel attacks, and prolonged strandings.
- International maritime law (UNCLOS, Maritime Labour Convention, San Remo Manual) and naval operations such as Operation Prosperity Guardian provide limited protection, as enforcement is weak, crews face multinational accountability gaps, and militarisation of distress channels and waterways endangers civilian lives and the environment.
- The crisis exposes a core contradiction in which global trade relies on roughly two million seafarers, many from developing countries, yet prioritises oil prices and strategic interests over their safety, evacuation rights, and human security, underscoring that freedom of navigation is incomplete without protecting those who sustain it.
The world’s oceans have become ever more dangerous for commercial shipping and the millions of seafarers who sustain international trade. The war in Ukraine, the continuing Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the military confrontation involving the United States, Israel and Iran have made some of the world’s busiest maritime routes into conflict zones. Merchant vessels carrying oil, food, fertilisers and other essential commodities have come under missile and drone attacks. Shipping companies have been forced to abandon traditional routes, while thousands of seafarers remain exposed to dangers over which they have little control.
The situation has deteriorated considerably since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February 2026. The subsequent confrontation has placed the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy corridors, at the centre of a growing maritime crisis. The consequences sprawl beyond rising oil prices, disrupted supply chains and higher insurance costs. They raise critical questions about the safety, dignity and rights of civilian seafarers caught in military conflicts.
From the Black Sea to the Persian Gulf
The maritime crisis acquired a new dimension following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The Black Sea became a major theatre of military operations, threatening commercial vessels transporting grain, energy and other commodities. The disruption of Ukrainian grain exports contributed to global food insecurity, particularly in countries dependent on imports from the region.
The Black Sea Grain Initiative, negotiated in July 2022 with the involvement of Türkiye and the United Nations, temporarily facilitated the movement of Ukrainian agricultural exports. However, Russia’s withdrawal from the agreement in July 2023 renewed uncertainty over commercial navigation. Missile attacks, naval mines and strikes on port infrastructure continued to threaten merchant vessels and their crews.
The war demonstrated how fast civilian shipping could become vulnerable when major powers resorted to military force. Seafarers from countries having no direct involvement in the conflict found themselves exposed to attacks, prolonged confinement and uncertainty over evacuation.
The crisis subsequently spread to another vital maritime region. Following the outbreak of the Gaza war in October 2023, Yemen’s Houthi movement began attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The Houthis presented their operations as part of their campaign against Israel and its supporters. However, attacks on merchant vessels placed civilian crews of different nationalities in danger.
The Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait form a crucial link between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal. Before the disruptions, the Suez route carried approximately 12–15 per cent of global maritime trade. Houthi attacks involving anti-ship missiles, drones and other weapons forced major shipping companies to divert vessels around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope. These diversions added thousands of nautical miles to voyages between Asia and Europe. Depending on the route, shipping times increased by one to two weeks. Additional fuel consumption, insurance premiums and operational expenses increased the cost of maritime transportation.
The effects were felt across the conflict zone and the countries dependent on imported food, energy and industrial materials faced additional costs. The longer voyages also increased greenhouse gas emissions, undermining efforts to reduce the environmental impact of international shipping.
The Strait of Hormuz: A Humanitarian Emergency
The confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the United States has created another serious crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. The narrow waterway connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. It is indispensable to the transportation of oil and liquefied natural gas from the Gulf. According to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), approximately 6,000 seafarers remained trapped aboard commercial vessels in the region in October 2026. The organisation’s Secretary-General, Arsenio Dominguez, described the situation as critical and warned that safe navigation could no longer be guaranteed. Reports published on 22–23 October indicated that the IMO had confirmed approximately 100 maritime incidents as of 9 October, while at least 24 seafarers had been killed since the conflict began on 28 February. Another 24 commercial vessels were reportedly attacked within approximately two weeks.
These figures reveal the seriousness of the situation. They also indicate the limitations of available information. The actual human consequences may be greater because smaller commercial vessels, fishing boats and other maritime workers are not always adequately represented in international reporting.
The attacks on the Singapore-registered vessels GFS Pride and GFS Giselle on 13 and 14 October validated the dangers. GFS Pride reportedly sank after being struck by a projectile, although its 21 crew members survived. GFS Giselle suffered hull damage, and its 22 crew members were evacuated. The immediate question concerns the fate of thousands of seafarers who remain stranded. They are unable to leave their vessels safely, return home or determine when normal commercial operations will resume. The IMO has advised shipping companies to avoid transiting the Strait until credible safety guarantees become available. Yet this warning provides little immediate relief to those already trapped in the conflict zone.
Seafarers as Victims of Geopolitical Conflicts
International maritime trade depends on approximately two million seafarers. A substantial proportion comes from developing countries, including India, the Philippines, Indonesia and other Asian nations. Their labour sustains the movement of commodities that support industrial production and everyday consumption across the world. However, seafarers remain among the most vulnerable workers during international conflicts. They spend long periods away from their families, often under difficult working conditions. When war breaks out, they face dangers that are unimaginable, going beyond the normal risks of maritime employment.
The current crisis has exposed them to missile attacks, drone strikes, naval mines, detention and prolonged confinement. Many experience anxiety over their families, uncertainty about wages and difficulties accessing medical assistance. Evacuation may become impossible when ports are closed or surrounding waters are militarised.
The multinational composition of commercial crews creates additional complications. A vessel may be owned by a company in one country, registered in another, operated from a third and staffed by workers from several countries. This complex arrangement makes accountability difficult when emergencies arise. For Indian seafarers, the crisis has particular significance. India is among the major suppliers of maritime labour to international shipping. Indian nationals serving aboard foreign-flagged vessels may be exposed to conflicts in which India has no military involvement. Their safety depends on shipping companies, flag states, coastal authorities and diplomatic intervention. When these institutions fail to coordinate, the seafarer becomes the weakest party in an increasingly complicated international system. The problem also concerns the right of workers to refuse dangerous assignments. Maritime employment should never require civilian workers to accept the possibility of death merely because commercial contracts must be fulfilled.
Maritime Law and Its Limitations
International law contains several provisions intended to protect commercial navigation and civilian seafarers. However, the present crisis has exposed serious weaknesses in their implementation. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) establishes important principles governing navigation. Article 87 recognises freedom of navigation on the high seas, while Article 38 provides for transit passage through straits used for international navigation. These provisions are essential to the functioning of international maritime trade. But they cannot, by themselves, prevent missile attacks, naval blockades or the seizure of commercial vessels.
International humanitarian law also requires parties to armed conflicts to distinguish between military objectives and civilian persons and objects. Merchant vessels ordinarily enjoy civilian protection, although they may lose protection against attack under specific circumstances recognised by the law of armed conflict. The United States’ war with Iran has no clear exit ramp. Periods of negotiation or reduced hostilities may interrupt the fighting, but they are unlikely to end the broader confrontation. Even if economic pressure forces change within the Iranian hierarchy, a more moderate leadership may not control much. And even if a cessation of hostilities holds, the asymmetric war is likely to continue.
For cyber defenders, that means the U.S. military, the defense industrial base (DIB) that supports it, and domestic critical infrastructure remain priority targets. Modern warfare is no longer limited to physical front lines. It has reached into corporate networks, industrial control systems, and the thousands of contractors and suppliers that sustain U.S. military operations.
Asymmetric war, asymmetric cyber
Iran’s military doctrine has long emphasized asymmetric tactics, from proxy militias and drone swarms to small boat harassment in the Strait of Hormuz. If you cannot match your adversary directly, force them to absorb pain across as many vectors as possible.
Cyber operations follow the same logic. The goal is not a decisive digital victory, but to impose economic costs, disrupt logistics, degrade industrial capacity, and generate friction everywhere at once.
Iran’s cyber effort includes dozens of loosely affiliated groups. ranging from state contractors to Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) proxies to freelance hacktivists. Their capabilities vary widely, but sophistication is beside the point. They move quickly, hit a large number of targets and do not stop. Collectively, they can cause significant disruption, and defenders have to answer all of it.
No more red lines
Iran built much of its cyber program around intelligence collection and influence operations, but it has repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to cause disruption. It targeted U.S. banks with distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks from 2011 to 2013, breached the control system of a New York dam in 2013, hit Las Vegas Sands with destructive wiper malware in 2014, and targeted Israeli-made controllers at dozens of U.S. facilities in 2023.
Historically, however, Iran stopped short of sustained attacks on American critical services because crossing certain thresholds risked military retaliation. However, this risk calculus has fundamentally changed. Iran’s leadership has been assassinated, the country repeatedly bombed, and its economy placed under enormous pressure. The regime is fighting for survival, and the escalation threshold has moved with it.
Iran’s recent attacks on U.S. water utilities are a clear sign that the gloves are coming off.
What does that mean in practice?
Fear of U.S. retaliation is less of a deterrent. Whatever punishment Washington devises now folds into pain Iran is already absorbing. Defenders should not plan around restraint that may no longer have a rational basis.
Iran does not need top-tier capabilities. Russia and China may be more sophisticated, but Iran has repeatedly breached critical infrastructure. When targets are soft, relatively crude attacks can be enough.
Iran is getting help. CrowdStrike detected a surge in Russian hacktivist activity supporting Tehran since the war began, including groups claiming attacks against U.S. networks.
The military supply chain is the real prize. Disrupting civilian infrastructure raises costs on the American public. But disrupting the logistics and industrial capacity supporting US military operations has direct battlefield value. This is what makes the defense industrial base a priority target.
An evolving threat landscape
State-directed attacks are targeting industrial control systems. In April 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Environmental Protection Agency, FBI, National Security Agency and other agencies warned that Iranian-affiliated actors were targeting internet-facing industrial equipment across government, water and energy systems, manipulating controls and causing operational disruption. By mid-August, utilities in at least 12 states had reported incidents, with some operators losing remote control and reverting to manual operations. The objective was not data theft, but disruption.
Additionally, ideologically aligned hacktivists are operating in parallel. They may be less sophisticated, but they can still halt production with ransomware or other relatively simple attacks. More importantly, they multiply Iran’s reach by hitting more targets while state teams focus on higher-value objectives. The two can also work in tandem, with criminal or hacktivist groups gaining initial access that more capable state actors can exploit. This means an intrusion that looks like ordinary cybercrime may be the opening move of something much bigger.
Another concern is the emergence of hybrid physical-cyber operations. Check Point tracked hundreds of Iranian attempts to compromise internet-connected cameras across countries experiencing missile activity. Iranian actors have also used cyber operations to locate military personnel and support kinetic targeting, while cyber-enabled surveillance and intelligence gathering have been tied to plots against U.S. officials and regime critics. Pro-Iranian hackers have also openly discussed targeting data centers supporting U.S. military communications and targeting systems.
Underlying all three is a pivot toward operational technology. Altering a programmable logic controller (PLC) does not simply expose information. It changes the physical world by slowing a production line, creating false readings, or disrupting manufacture of components destined for weapons systems.
The supply chain is the battlefield
Major primes have the resources and regulatory pressure to run meaningful security programs. The thousands of small- and mid-sized subcontractors feeding into them often do not. If the objective is to degrade military-industrial capacity, those weaker nodes are attractive precisely because they connect to more hardened targets.
A compromised managed service provider can provide access to dozens of downstream facilities. A supplier with legitimate credentials can become an open door into a prime’s network. Iranian operators are mapping these relationships, harvesting credentials, and looking for the connective tissue between organizations. A defense contractor’s security posture is no longer just its own problem.
Defending against the threat
None of this requires becoming a cyber fortress overnight, but every defense contractor should reassess whether its cybersecurity reflects today’s threat environment or the one that existed five years ago.
Begin with the threat model. If your program is built primarily around protecting intellectual property, you are defending the last war. The objective now may be disruption or destruction. Iranian operators frequently use wiper malware and may also weaponize ransomware. Assume an attack could be intended to delete data, disrupt operations or damage systems, and build your recovery plans accordingly.
Treat operational technology (OT) security as seriously as IT security. Know your supply chain well enough to identify the weakest links, because adversaries are mapping them too. Monitor continuously rather than checking compliance boxes periodically.
Expect simultaneous and overlapping attacks. State units, proxies, hacktivists, and criminal crews may work together. A proxy may gain initial access and hand it off to a state-backed team, while Iranian actors have also brokered access to ransomware affiliates and paid criminals to hit U.S. and Israeli targets. State operations can also masquerade as ordinary cybercrime. What looks like a criminal attack may be the opening move of something much larger.
Don’t stop your Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) efforts. Phase 2 may be paused, but the threat isn’t. Our research mapped 130 techniques used by five Iranian threat groups against the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Special Publication 800-171 baseline. Sixty-eight percent can be mitigated by controls already in it, and 100% can be detected with the right monitoring. Four controls carry most of that weight: system monitoring, configuration settings, baseline configuration and malicious code protection.
The conflict with Iran is a stark demonstration of what modern asymmetric warfare looks like. What Iran is demonstrating through these attacks will not stay with Iran. China, Russia, and other U.S. adversaries are watching. Defense contractors should plan accordingly.

articles.title: North Korea may be the biggest winner of Russia’s war in Ukraine - Atlantic Council
articles.summary: North Korea may be the biggest winner of Russia’s war in Ukraine  Atlantic Council
articles.full_text:
OMAHA—While ostensibly not a belligerent party to Russia’s war against Ukraine, North Korea may emerge as one of the conflict’s largest beneficiaries. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv seem closer to finding an end to the war even if a three-way peace talk comes to fruition, and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s most recent public statements have largely repeated demands that have remained unchanged throughout 2026. Yet North Korea’s role supporting Russia in the war has already yielded substantial gains.
North Korean People’s Army troops started deploying to Russia in October 2024, following the signing of the partnership framework between Pyongyang and Moscow in June of that year. North Korean military activity remains cloaked in secrecy and the exact terms of the Russia–North Korea support agreement are unknown. However, Pyongyang benefits substantially and strategically from combat experience, weapons sales, battlefield testing of its systems, financing, and possibly technology transfers. These gains could extend beyond the war, strengthening North Korea’s military capabilities and potentially altering the strategic security equation in the Indo-Pacific.
What does North Korea gain?
By sending its troops to help Russia, North Korea firstly gains combat experience. Its army has not fought a significant engagement since 1953, and the North Korean deployment to Kursk represents the first opportunity for a generation of soldiers and commanders to learn the hard lessons of actual combat. Reports indicate that North Korea has deployed approximately eleven thousand troops to Russia, and Ukrainian military intelligence stated in August that an additional thirty thousand to fifty thousand North Korean troops could soon arrive. In all, the Institute for the Study of War estimates that roughly twenty-five thousand North Korean troops have rotated through the Russian theater since the deployment began. So far, these forces have been mostly used for border security. But if Ukrainian estimates of looming increases are correct, then the additional forces could free Russian forces for additional offensive actions, which could place additional strain on already stretched Ukrainian defenses.
Beyond combat experience, weapons exports and combat testing of indigenously produced weapons are the next area of significant operational, tactical, and strategic gain for Pyongyang. Testing under combat conditions yields significantly better engineering data and real-time improvements. In fact, North Korea may already be implementing battlefield-learned improvements. According to an early 2025 report, North Korean ballistic missile accuracy had improved since the beginning of the deployment. Japanese public broadcaster NHK separately reported that Moscow had pledged further assistance in drone and counter-drone technology to the North Koreans in exchange for their continued support. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that North Korea has exported fifteen million artillery shells to Russia since 2022. Ukrainian intelligence has stated that, at points in the war, up to 40 percent of Russian artillery consumption came from North Korean factories. And an article in The Korea Times, citing South Korean Defense Intelligence, reported that North Korea has sent some 33,000 shipping containers containing munitions, self-propelled guns, rocket launchers, and short range ballistic missiles to Russia.
Feedback from these arms transfers will likely improve the quality of North Korean weapons and boost the North Korean arms industry. It will also likely improve engineering and quality control, and could result in reciprocal transfers of sanctioned and embargoed technology that North Korea currently lacks. The full extent of the benefits are impossible to quantify, but dollar figures can be estimated for some aspects of the partnership. For example, reporting indicates that Russia has paid North Korea up to $13 billion for its military assistance. In August, Bloomberg placed the broader sanctions-evasion windfall for Pyongyang as high as $22 billion.
It is critical to understand not only what material is leaving North Korea, but also what is coming in. Technological transfers from Russia may include everything from space-related technology to precision-strike improvements, both of which have long limited North Korean capabilities. Shortly before the partnership was signed in June 2024, North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un traveled to a Russian space launch facility in the Russian far east. At the time, US officials warned that Russia could share satellite and space-launch technology—capabilities that North Korea struggles to produce domestically—in exchange for munitions and manpower. While there is no public evidence that Russia has directly contributed to North Korea’s nuclear weapons program, it is plausible that the by-products of such technology transfers could benefit Pyongyang’s weapons research and development programs.
Nuclear propulsion may be another matter. In late 2025, Kim unveiled the hull of North Korea’s first nuclear-powered submarine. This may have been enabled by Russian assistance and, if it becomes fully operational, could significantly improve North Korean nuclear capabilities. In addition, South Korean officials have asserted that Russia has transferred air-defense missile systems to North Korea. All of this taken together, North Korea’s support for Russia has likely helped Pyongyang close several important technological gaps that it has long struggled with under sanctions and isolation.
Implications for the United States and Indo-Pacific
Most estimates put Russian casualties in the war above a million and growing at thousands per month. Ukraine, too, has sustained significant losses. It is costing hundreds of billions of dollars to sustain the war effort, and the economic damage is running into the trillions of dollars. Recovery will take decades, assuming a stable peace is able to be reached.
North Korea, by contrast, has entered a European war at limited direct cost. It has not risked confrontation with its principal adversaries while gaining strategic leverage and greatly improving its military capabilities. Its partnership with Russia, Pyongyang’s most formal security arrangement with Moscow since the Soviet era, has given it a new form of strategic insurance. It has also weakened multilateral arms-transfer sanctions and enforcement and made it far more difficult for the United States and United Nations to track and expose sanctions-evasion networks.
The consequences for Indo-Pacific partners may play out over decades. Once isolated and largely constrained by China, Kim may now feel emboldened to pursue his regional objectives vis-à-vis South Korea and Japan. The combination of Pyongyang’s increased capabilities and now battle-hardened forces could raise North Korean confidence in its own strategic decision-making, thus potentially increasing the baseline risk for Northern miscalculation on the peninsula, or even with its neighbors and the United States. This could take many forms, including clashes in disputed areas to a new round of “missile coercion” by North Korea.
Many questions remain. What is China’s calculus regarding North Korea’s advancing capabilities? Beijing values stability on the peninsula, and a loss of leverage on Kim is unlikely to be seen by Chinese officials as a positive development. Critically, how enduring is the “unlimited partnership” with Russia, particularly if the exigencies of the war in Ukraine come to an end? What does it mean for US strategic planning and contingency responses? For nuclear deterrence?
