articles.summary: Sicily earthquakes live: Tsunami warning for Italy after 12 quakes near Palermo  Daily MirrorTsunami alert issued in Italy after 12 earthquakes hit Mediterranean coastline  The IndependentTsunami alert issued after swarm of nearly 3 dozen earthquakes rattle the Tyrrhenian Sea off the Italian coast  FOX WeatherEarthquake in Sicily, seismic swarm in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea: orange tsunami alert - LIVE  Agenzia NovaShallow Aeolian Swarm Triggers Tsunami A...
articles.full_text:
A tsunami warning remains in place after a series of 12 earthquakes struck off the coast of Sicily.
The tremors occurred close to Palermo, with the strongest registering a magnitude of 5.0 and striking at around 12:19pm local time. The epicentre was in the southern Tyrrhenian Sea north-west of the Aeolian Islands.
Schools and government buildings have been evacuated in Palermo, the capital of Sicily, as well as in Messina following the orange tsunami alert. Locals poured out onto streets fearing buildings would collapse, with authorities checking residences for structural damage.
Prior to the 5.0 magnitude quake, a 4.3 magnitude tremor occurred at 11:51am. As many as 10 other earthquakes in the area today had a magnitude of at least 3 - and authorities have warned more aftershocks could follow.
The earthquake swarm is linked to the African tectonic plate pushing against the Eurasian plate beneath the Mediterranean, putting pressure on the Earth's crust around Sicily, according to experts.
Seismologist Nicola Alessandro Pino told Fanpage.it: "A well-known seismic zone has been activated, linked to the compression of the African plate on the Eurasian plate."
What does the orange tsunami warning mean?
Italy's national tsunami warning system classifies an orange warning as "advisory" - meaning coastal communities could be impacted by a tsunami wave of less than 0.5 metres and/or a maximum run-up on land of less than one metre.
However, the issuing of the alert does not necessarily mean a tsunami will strike the region.
Residents urged to remain alert amid further tremors
Authorities have urged residents to remain vigilant amid the risk of further earthquakes, with municipalities told to take precautions in vulnerable buildings and busy public spaces.
The region has also called on local authorities to report the prevention measures they have introduced, while residents are being urged to follow official updates from Civil Protection and Italy's National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV).
Everything we know so far
A series of earthquakes struck the southern Tyrrhenian Sea off Sicily today, with tremors felt across parts of the Island, including Palermo and the Aolian Islands. Here's what we know so far:
- The tremors sparked panic across Sicily, with frightened residents rushing out of buildings and into the streets amid fears they could collapse.
- The strongest quake recorded today reached magnitude 5.5 at 12:19pm local time, with its epicentre at the sea near the Aolian Islands.
- A further magnitude 4.6 earthquake was recorded at 3:55pm, followed by another tremor measuring 4.1 at 5:32pm, according to local reports.
- An orange tsunami alert was issued following the strongest tremor but lifted around an hour later after monitoring ruled out major changes in sea level.
- Sicily's regional civil protection department has urged municipalities to check vulnerable buildings, with particular attention to schools, hospitals, bridges and other public structures.
- All schools and universities in Palermo will remain closed until Sunday morning as a precaution.
No injuries reported
There have been no reports of any injuries from the earthquakes today, but a rock face has reportedly collapsed on Filicudi, one of the Aeolian Islands.
Authorities have been checking residences in affected areas for structural damage.
Latest seismic activity follows string of earthquakes in same area
The latest seismic activity comes after a series of earthquakes in the same area. Seven tremors, the strongest measuring magnitude 3.7, were reported off the coast of Sicily on Thursday.
Roads and highways undergo inspections
Specialist technicians have carried out inspections of roads and highways across Palermo and Messina, paying close attention to bridges, viaducts and tunnels.
ANAS, the state-controlled road infrastructure company, said the inspections were aimed at spotting any anomalies or damage linked to the quakes.
Staff have so far found no major damage and ANAS says it will continue to monitor the situation.
Locals gripped by fear amid quakes
People, gripped by fear, took to the streets amid the quakes, La Repubblica reports. Students in schools across the city were evacuated from their classrooms into the safety of school courtyard meanwhile public offices and facilities were also evacuated.
Palermo’s mayor, Roberto Lagalla, said immediately after the quakes: “We are monitoring the situation’s development with the utmost attention, in constant coordination with all relevant authorities. At present, there have been no reports of harm to people or property; however, we believe it is our duty to take every necessary step to ensure the safety of our citizens. The potential evacuation of certain public facilities is a purely precautionary measure, prompted by the need to act both promptly and prudently."
'Everything started shaking'
Palermo residents have described the moment their homes began shaking after a multiple earthquakes rocked the city today.
"Sorry, can someone in Palermo tell me if they felt the earthquake? I was sitting down and everything started shaking," one X user said.
Another added: "Well, we just had a 5.0 earthquake here in Palermo. It definitely wasn't pleasant up on the 6th floor - I thought I was sick or something!"
Quake comes after 'unprecedented' Sicily tornado left two seriously injured
Today's earthquakes come after a tornado ripped through the Sicilian city of Marsala and neighbouring towns earlier this month.
The twister, described by experts as unprecedented for the Mediterranean island, left vehicles overturned and two people seriously injured. A house and school were among the buildings damaged amid the chaos.
"It was almost like an American tornado, nothing this violent has been seen in living memory," the head of Sicily's civil protection agency Salvatore Cocina told Reuters.
All schools and universities to remain closed until Sunday
Palermo Mayor Roberto Lagalla has signed an ordinance ordering all schools and universities to close until 8am on Sunday as a precautionary measure.
The move will also see municipal Civil Protection units activated, as well as an increased local police presence. The measures are in effect until 8am on Sunday, "unless further provisions are made."
'I'm absolutely terrified'
Palermo residents have described their fear after a series of earthquakes struck near the city earlier today, with some forced to evacuate buildings.
Posting to X, one person said: "I'm absolutely terrified but fortunately everything's fine". Another resident added: "Honestly, I totally lost it down there, they even evacuated us from the building."
Safety checks to be carried out at schools, hospitals, and public buildings
Municipalities in Palermo and Messina are being asked to carry out safety checks on schools, hospitals, and other public buildings following today's earthquakes.
The warning was sent by the Regional Civil Protection Agency, with mayors and managers of public and private facilities asked to verify their safety before using them.
Authorities are being urged to pay particular attention to buildings that have already been damaged or are more vulnerable.
Eight more tremors recorded as 4.1 magnitude quake strikes
A further eight mini tremors were recorded in southern Tyrrhenian Sea between 4.05pm and 4.51pm local time, with magnitudes ranging from 2.1 to 2.9, according to Giornale de Sicilia.
Another earthquake was then reported at 5:32pm, measuring magnitude 4.1. The exact location of the latest quake has not yet been confirmed.
African plate pushing against Europe linked to Sicily earthquake swarm
The earthquakes are linked to two giant tectonic plates pushing against each other beneath the Mediterranean, an expert has said.
Seismologist Nicola Alessandro Pino, a former senior researcher at Italy's National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV), said the African plate is slowly pushing into the Eurasian plate, putting pressure on the Earth's crust and triggering seismic activity around Sicily. She told Fanpage.it:
A well-known seismic zone has been activated, linked to the compression of the African plate on the Eurasian plate.
Checks ordered on vulnerable buildings
Salvatore Cocina, director of the Sicilian Regional Civil Protection Department, has sent a directive to municipalities urging them to check the stability of the most vulnerable buildings and monitor coastal areas following the earthquakes.
Classes at University of Palermo cancelled
Classes at the University of Palermo have been suspended for the day following this morning's earthquake. A message on the university's website reads:
Due to the seismic event that occurred on October 23, 2026, all teaching activities scheduled for that day are suspended with immediate effect for safety reasons.
Schools have also been evacuated in the neighboring coastal municipalities of Trabia and Altavilla.
Tsunami alert lifted
The orange tsunami alert has been lifted as no changes in sea level were detected, reports La Sicilia.
The latest quake, which had a magnitude of 4.6, was felt at 3:55pm local time in the Aeolian Islands and in Palermo, according to the INGV.
New tremor hits Aeolian Islands and Palermo
A new strong earthquake was felt at 3:55pm local time in the Aeolian Islands and in Palermo, reports Giornale de Sicilia.
A provisional estimate from the INGV says the quake had a magnitude between 5.0 and 5.5. The magnitude was later revised to 4.6.
Why Sicily is prone to earthquakes
Sicily lies within the Mediterranean seismic belt - an area particularly vulnerable to earthquakes due to the movement of tectonic plates beneath the Earth's surface.
The Italian island was devastated by the 1693 Val di Noto earthquake, one of the deadliest in European history. The magnitude 7.4 quake destroyed towns and villages across eastern Sicily and is estimated to have killed 60,000 people.

articles.title: Melissa Parke, ICAN executive director: ‘The risk of nuclear war has never been higher than it is today’ - EL PAÍS English
articles.summary: Melissa Parke, ICAN executive director: ‘The risk of nuclear war has never been higher than it is today’  EL PAÍS English
articles.full_text:
Humanity has never been closer to self-destruction. That is the warning of the Doomsday Clock, an initiative the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists updates each year to alert the public to threats facing the planet. It is now only 85 seconds to midnight—the symbol of total annihilation—because of the climate emergency, the rise of artificial intelligence and wars threatening millions of people. Moreover, amid a surge in militarism, the world’s most powerful countries have accelerated an arms race to expand and modernize their nuclear arsenals, which is why the Doomsday Clock was first unveiled in 1947.
“We are exposing humanity to the risk of a nuclear war which can end the world in an afternoon,” says Melissa Parke, 60, executive director of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN). The coalition, made up of more than 700 NGOs, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2017 for pushing the United Nations to adopt the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. However, the nine states that possess nuclear weapons— the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom, France, India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel (which neither confirms nor denies its arsenal)—have not joined the treaty. Other NATO members have not joined either.
“No one would survive a nuclear war. It’s suicide,” says this Australian expert, responding to those in Europe who defend building their own atomic arsenal. In an interview in Madrid, Clarke reviewed the comings and goings of Donald Trump, threats from the Kremlin, the dangers posed by the military use of artificial intelligence, and conflicts in Europe and the Middle East, a region to which she has devoted more than a decade of her professional career.
Question. What factors are driving us toward a nuclear catastrophe?
Answer. The risk of nuclear war has never been higher than it is today. We have two major conflicts started by countries with nuclear weapons: Russia, and the United States and Israel. We have a complete breakdown in arms control agreements. There are nuclear threats being made, a new arms race underway and, on top of that, we hear very disturbing rhetoric from European leaders who, despite asserting their commitment to the Non‑Proliferation Treaty, are talking about nuclear rearmament.
I was at the Munich Security Conference and heard [Spain’s Prime Minister] Pedro Sánchez deliver a brilliant speech. Surrounded by militarist hawks, he pushed back against nuclear rearmament, called it a historic error and questioned the logic of nuclear deterrence. He said that a system that requires zero risk and zero errors to avoid total destruction is not a guarantee but a gamble. He is right. If we have avoided a nuclear war it has been by sheer luck, but we cannot rely on that luck to last forever. As the UN secretary‑general [António Guterres] says, when it comes to nuclear weapons, luck is not a strategy.
Despite Sánchez’s words, Spain’s policies have not lived up to those speeches and remain tied to NATO’s nuclear umbrella. But that is not inherent to Alliance membership; it is a political choice. What we ask is that they act in accordance with their principles. NATO’s current policy strikes me as counterproductive. It is pushing Europe toward war instead of away from it.
Last year tensions between India and Pakistan almost turned into a nuclear conflict because of AI‑generated deepfake videos
Q. What risks does integrating artificial intelligence into nuclear arsenals pose?
A. AI is increasingly being incorporated into nuclear weapons systems, which is absolutely terrifying. This spring we saw the United States mobilizing its military based on an intelligence report claiming a Chinese ship was transporting nuclear components bound for Iran. At the last minute they discovered that information came from an AI that was hallucinating. That is how easily a nuclear war can start.
Last year tensions between India and Pakistan almost turned into a nuclear conflict because of AI‑generated deepfake videos showing leaders saying things they never said, in addition to mass disinformation campaigns produced by artificial intelligence. And just days ago, AI agents hacked into Australia’s public healthcare system. The people developing AI do not have control over it. Integrating these technologies into nuclear weapons is a recipe for disaster.
Q. Is this arms race inevitable or is it still possible to impose controls?
A. Arms control is necessary in the short term, but we have to stop merely managing these weapons and move toward their elimination. We saw this with the New START agreement [the last nuclear treaty between Russia and the United States, which expired this year]: when trust ends and agreements end, the nuclear weapons remain. Every day that passes without eliminating them, we are exposing humanity to the risk of a nuclear war which can end the world in an afternoon.
A lot of people think the danger from nuclear weapons went away with the end of the Cold War. It did not. The weapons are far more powerful now. Of the roughly 12,000 warheads that exist, about 4,000 remain on on high alert launch status. That means political leaders would have to react within minutes to verify whether the information they receive—perhaps generated by AI—is accurate. A catastrophic miscalculation is just any time around the corner.
Q. The conflict in the Middle East has revived fears about Iran’s atomic program and Israel’s nuclear arsenal. Do you consider the use of nuclear weapons a real risk?
A. In both Ukraine and Iran, nuclear weapons have been strategically irrelevant. They have not prevented wars nor stopped Ukraine and Iran from responding to attacks. But they have been sitting in the background dramatically increasing the stakes of every miscalculation.
Israel has nuclear weapons. It is the only country in the Middle East that possesses them. It is ironic that you have two nuclear-armed states, the U.S. and Israel, that have attacked a non-nuclear-armed state on the basis of its alleged nuclear weapons program, which the U.S.’s own intelligence agencies and the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) have confirmed does not have a nuclear weapons program.
If the concern is proliferation, attention should be turned to the country which does have nuclear weapons and which does not submit to any international safeguards and any inspections by the IAEA, and that’s Israel. It’s as if these nuclear weapons are giving them a sense of impunity and unaccountability in international law, and that’s also not acceptable.
Q. Do you think the upcoming elections in Israel will affect the conflict?
A. Unfortunately, even if Benjamin Netanyahu left power, there are many others who would continue the same policies. Netanyahu should appear before The Hague to face war crime charges, but I do not see candidates likely to win who will have a different policy. The U.S. is the country that has the most influence over Israel. If it chose to, it could stop what is happening. It has not chosen to.
Q. Trump said a few days ago that he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran. What do you make of that?
A. At the UN General Assembly he explicitly issued a nuclear threat against Iran. He said they could be “annihilated” quickly. He also said something similar earlier this year when he posted a message saying “an entire civilization will die tonight.” However, he appears convinced of what he calls “denuclearization” and of the need to engage in dialogue with Russia and China. He also appears convinced that nuclear weapons are very dangerous and wasteful of resources. At the same time, his actions are not matching his words. The United States continues full steam ahead to expand and modernize its arsenals.
Q. As the Kremlin ratchets up the tone of its threats and the United States seems a less reliable ally, many European countries maintain that nuclear deterrence is the only alternative. What would you tell them?
A. I would tell them they’ll be the first ones to go in a nuclear war. No one would survive a nuclear war. It is not a protection; it is suicide. It is like living in a house of dynamite. You never know when it will blow up.
Q. What can be done about countries with opaque nuclear programs, such as Israel, North Korea or China?
A. At the height of the Cold War there were some 70,000 nuclear weapons. After the agreements between Mikhail Gorbachev and Ronald Reagan, that figure was reduced to roughly 12,000 today. That shows we know how to do it, in a verifiable, time-bound way.
Of all the major global challenges we face, this one is probably the least complex. It is a matter of political will and leadership. What would likely be needed is a multilateral agreement to reduce arsenals, monitored by an independent body such as the IAEA. Of course, countries like Israel and North Korea would need security guarantees assuring them that their existence is not threatened. That can be achieved.
Q. You head an organization that has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. What do you think of Trump’s push to receive one?
A. Trump has waged war, so I think he is a long way from deserving it. If he were to take the initiative to eliminate nuclear weapons in the world, that indeed would be worthy of a Nobel. He should think about that.

articles.title: North Korea Is Using Experience From Russia's War Against Ukraine to Improve Its Missiles and Drones - SFG Media
articles.summary: North Korea Is Using Experience From Russia's War Against Ukraine to Improve Its Missiles and Drones  SFG Media
articles.full_text:
By supplying weapons and deploying troops to Russia, North Korea has gained valuable data on how its military technology performs under real combat conditions. According to Anton Ponomarenko, a researcher at Pacific Forum, analyzing battlefield performance is helping Pyongyang improve warhead accuracy and missile maneuverability, making the threat to South Korea more serious.
		
			North Korea is focusing on developing more powerful warheads and missiles capable of penetrating modern missile defense systems. It is also working to shorten launch preparations and make its launchers harder to detect.
		
			The rivalry between the two countries intensified this month with a series of missile tests. North Korea fired a ballistic missile it described as a nuclear-capable hypersonic weapon, with Kim Jong Un personally observing the launch.
		
			South Korean and Japanese military officials estimated that the missile traveled approximately 430 miles. Pyongyang, however, claimed a range of 621 miles, attributing the discrepancy to a warhead that followed an unpredictable trajectory at several times the speed of sound. North Korea said this prevented neighboring countries from tracking the entire flight.
		
			Five days later, South Korea conducted its own test of a hypersonic ballistic missile, observed by President Lee Jae-myung. Rather than following its usual practice of merely condemning North Korean missile tests, Seoul demonstrated its own military capabilities.
		
			The presidential office also released a photograph of Lee inspecting the Hyunmoo-5 missile system. The missile is reportedly equipped with an eight-ton warhead designed to destroy underground fortifications and facilities that could shelter enemy leaders.
		
			Four days after that inspection, North Korea tested a missile that analysts identified as a weapon designed to strike fortified underground targets. It is believed to be capable of carrying a payload weighing up to 2.5 tons.
		
			The tests followed another escalation of tensions along the inter-Korean border. Last month, three South Korean soldiers were wounded by land mines that Seoul says North Korean forces had planted south of the poorly marked boundary. The incident was followed by warning shots and exchanges of threats.
		
			Beyond missiles, Pyongyang is devoting increasing attention to unmanned systems. According to Ukrainian officials, Russia has recruited 12,000 North Korean workers to manufacture Geran-2 drones at facilities in Tatarstan. Russian officers have also been sent to North Korea to train drone operators.
		
			Photographs released after Kim Jong Un visited a drone manufacturing facility last month also point to an expansion of domestic production. The images suggest that North Korea has already begun mass-producing such aircraft.
		
			During separate military exercises, North Korean forces demonstrated their ability to deploy several types of weapons simultaneously. Drones attacked a target on an island while cruise and ballistic missiles approached it from different directions.
		
			Military experts warn that such tactics could force South Korea and its allies to undertake costly upgrades to their air defense systems. The use of relatively inexpensive attack weapons compels defenders to expend far more expensive resources to intercept them.
		
			"We will see a widening imbalance between inexpensive offensive weapons and costly defensive systems," said Hong Min, an analyst at the Korea Institute for National Unification.
		
			Changes in how North Korea deploys and launches its missiles present another challenge for South Korea's military. Pyongyang is developing submarine-based systems, using mobile launchers concealed in tunnels and shifting toward solid-fuel missiles that require less preparation before launch.
		
			Some North Korean missiles can also carry either conventional or nuclear warheads. This complicates threat assessments after a launch is detected, since South Korean commanders cannot always determine what type of weapon the North has deployed.
		
			South Korea's deterrence strategy continues to rely on the presence of US forces and the American nuclear arsenal. Seoul's own military program remains focused primarily on developing conventional weapons for preemptive strikes, missile interception and large-scale retaliatory operations.
		
			In an interview with The New York Times last month, President Lee Jae-myung said that any North Korean use of nuclear weapons in an attack would lead to the country's destruction.
		
			"Using them for offensive purposes would guarantee the North's self-destruction," he said.
		
			South Korea retains an advantage over the North in air and naval power and coordinates intelligence surveillance with Washington. However, advances in North Korean weapons are gradually eroding Seoul's superiority in certain areas. Meanwhile, recent South Korean drone tests have suffered setbacks.
		
			Against this backdrop, the South Korean government has pledged to increase defense spending from 2.8% to 3.5% of gross domestic product.
		
			Another concern is how Russian-North Korean military cooperation could affect US commitments to defend South Korea. According to Lami Kim of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, if Moscow's assistance enables Pyongyang to develop reliable capabilities for launching nuclear strikes against American cities, Washington could become more cautious when deciding whether to intervene militarily to defend its ally.

Other Russian officials meanwhile demonstrated Russia’s unwillingness to make any meaningful concessions toward ending the war in Ukraine. These are similar to the Kremlin’s earlier negotiation tactics which tried to convince the United States and the West generally that Ukrainian defenses were going to collapse such that Ukraine should preemptively capitulate.[6]
The Kremlin is fundamentally interested only in buying time to resolve the war on the battlefield while Russia simultaneously reaps the benefits of economic cooperation with the United States. articles.summary: Tensions Along Eritrea-Ethiopia Border Risk Erupting Into War  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- Eritrean troops reportedly crossed into northern Ethiopia near Zalambessa around 7 October, prompting Ethiopia to accuse its neighbor of a 60-kilometer incursion and to launch drone strikes on Eritrean military vehicles near Adi Grat the following day.
- The International Crisis Group and other analysts warn that the standoff risks escalating into interstate war over the border and the port of Assab, potentially drawing in regional actors, amid incomplete implementation of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement.
- Experts outline three scenarios—continued Eritrean support for Ethiopian armed groups, a proxy stalemate, or full-scale war—and urge immediate de-escalation given the millions still displaced or in need of aid from the previous conflict.
Troop movements, drone attacks and escalating rhetoric have pushed Eritrea and Ethiopia back to the brink of war. Analysts warn that, without a drastic reversal, the conflict risks costing thousands of lives and drawing in countries from across the region.
Experts are pointing to the two countries’ devastating history of border conflict and are urging a diplomatic solution.
“A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events,” the International Crisis Group (ICG) wrote in an October 12 assessment. “The last major interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa, in which hundreds of thousands perished in trench warfare, was fought along precisely the same border.”
Witness accounts and independent monitors reported that Eritrean troops crossed the border in northern Ethiopia near the town of Zalambessa on about October 7. In a letter to the United Nations Security Council, the Ethiopian government accused its northern neighbor of sending troops 60 kilometers into its territory.
Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence.”
In response, Ethiopia launched drone attacks against Eritrean military vehicles near the town of Adi Grat on October 8, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project, or ACLED. Ethiopia has also deployed forces to the north and retaken several towns that had been held by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), a political party and armed group that has recently aligned with Eritrea.
The tensions follow a period of weeks when several of Ethiopia’s armed groups including the TPLF and the Fano, an ethnically Amhara militia, launched attacks against Ethiopian federal government positions. Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of supporting these groups with arms and training.
Eritrea has reason to fear that landlocked Ethiopia has ambitions to invade and occupy the port city of Assab to gain access to the Red Sea. Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki appears to believe he can protect his country by arming rebels inside Ethiopia.
“For Eritrea, continued conflict inside Ethiopia reduces the threat to Assab,” Hafte Gebreselassie Gebrihet, a research fellow at the University of Oslo, wrote for The Conversation. “A federal government fighting in the Amhara, Oromia and Tigray regions has fewer troops, less money and less political space to pressure Eritrea.”
The tensions come nearly four years after the signing of the Pretoria Agreement which formally ended Ethiopia’s civil war with the TPLF. However, Hafte writes, the agreement has not been implemented in a way that would guarantee lasting peace. The disputed territory of Western Tigray has not been returned to Tigrayan administration, the northern region of Tigray has not been reintegrated into federal politics, and the promised disarmament of militias has stalled.
The failure of Pretoria makes groups less likely to disarm and gives outside actors like Eritrea an opening to form alliances and destabilize Ethiopia, Hafte argued.
“Peace in Tigray depends on making implementation more valuable than continued uncertainty,” Hafte wrote.
In an article written for the New Humanitarian, journalist Daniel Berhane wrote that there are three possible scenarios for the conflict in northern Ethiopia and Eritrea.
- Armed groups proliferate: Eritrea stops sending troops across the border but continues to support armed groups like the TPLF and Fano.
- A stalemate: the northern region continues to be a proxy-conflict with insurgents controlling parts of the countryside and the federal government controlling population centers.
- Interstate war: Ethiopia and Eritrea return to war over unresolved border issues and control of the port of Assab. The war would likely draw in regional nations and Gulf states.
Experts are urging deescalation, noting that a million people are still displaced from the last conflict and four million require aid. The humanitarian toll of a return to conflict could be much worse.
“Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea back from the brink of war should be the priority for all those interested in preventing a deadly chain of interconnected conflicts from snaking across the Horn of Africa and Red Sea regions,” the ICG wrote.

The European Union warns that AI-generated deepfakes and manipulated media could mislead millions of voters ahead of Nigeria's 2027 general elections, while INEC explores using AI to reduce errors in election result management by matching electronically entered figures with paper result sheets.
The European Union has warned that AI-generated fake news could threaten the credibility of the 2027 general elections, as the Independent National Electoral Commission explores the use of artificial intelligence to reduce errors in election result management.
The EU, through its Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria Programme, said manipulated images, videos and audio recordings could mislead millions of voters. Experts cautioned that the technology could also be exploited to manipulate public opinion and undermine confidence in the electoral process. INEC, however, said its proposed AI application would help ensure that electronically entered figures match those on paper result sheets before transmission.

The European Union Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria Programme, while raising concerns over the growing threat of Artificial Intelligence-generated fake news ahead of the 2027 general elections, warned that manipulated images, videos and audio recordings could mislead millions of Nigerians. The programme said electoral institutions, media organisations, technology platforms and citizens needed to strengthen their preparedness to identify and respond to disinformation as the country approaches the polls.
Speaking on behalf of the EU-SDGN Programme, Lanre Arogundade said on Thursday in a statement by the EU-SDGN that advances in Artificial Intelligence had made it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic electoral information from fabricated content.
“The challenge before us is no longer simply whether false information can influence elections. Artificial Intelligence has made it possible to produce convincing images, videos and audio recordings capable of misleading millions of people within minutes,” Arogundade said. He said Nigeria needed to assess whether its electoral institutions, the media, technology platforms and citizens were adequately prepared to tackle the emerging threats.
“As Nigeria approaches the 2027 elections, we must ask whether our electoral institutions, the media, technology platforms and citizens are sufficiently prepared to recognise and respond to these threats,” he added. Arogundade spoke ahead of a two-day national summit scheduled for November 2 and 3, 2026, at the Abuja Continental Hotel.
The summit, titled “Beyond the Ballot: Safeguarding Electoral Information Integrity in the Age of AI,” is being organised by the International Press Centre and the Centre for Media and Society, in collaboration with DAI and International IDEA, under the EU-SDGN Programme, funded by the European Union. According to the organisers, the summit will bring together approximately 250 participants, including representatives of the Independent National Electoral Commission, media organisations, technology platforms, fact-checking groups, civil society organisations, government institutions and academia.
The meeting will examine how AI-generated deepfakes, manipulated images, coordinated disinformation campaigns and foreign information manipulation and interference could distort electoral information, influence public perceptions and undermine confidence in election outcomes. A major feature of the summit will be an interactive simulation of an AI-driven electoral disinformation crisis, designed to test how institutions and information actors respond when misleading content spreads during an election.
Arogundade said the gathering was intended to move beyond discussions about information disorder and identify practical measures to protect the integrity of electoral information.
“Beyond the Ballot is not just another conference about information disorder. It is an opportunity to test our preparedness, examine institutional responsibilities and identify practical measures to protect the integrity of electoral information.
“Our objective is to ensure that Nigerians can make electoral decisions based on credible information rather than manipulation, deception or manufactured narratives,” he said. The summit will also examine the responsibilities of digital platforms, the influence of social media content creators, the implications of foreign information manipulation and interference, and the evolving role of journalism in an AI-driven information environment.
Participants are expected to discuss strategies for detecting manipulated content, verifying election-related claims, communicating accurate information during electoral emergencies and strengthening public resilience against disinformation. The discussions will also consider how to protect electoral information integrity while safeguarding freedom of expression, media independence and citizens’ right to information. The concerns come as Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections, when political campaigns and voter engagement are expected to rely heavily on digital communication platforms.
INEC, however, said it was deploying AI to curb errors in election result management ahead of the 2027 general election. Speaking at the launch of the AI for Elections Programme and Hackathon organised by Rise Networks in Abuja, INEC Director of Information and Communication Technology, Lawrence Bayode, said the commission was exploring practical uses of AI while putting safeguards in place to ensure its responsible deployment.
Explaining how the technology would work in the result management system, he said: “The system checks whether the figures entered electronically match those on the paper result sheets and scanned copies before transmission is allowed. If discrepancies exist, they must be resolved before the results can be uploaded. ” Bayode said the initiative would help minimise human errors, enhance operational efficiency and ensure that figures published on INEC’s portal correspond with results recorded at polling units.
He cautioned, however, that technological advancement must not undermine electoral security, operational stability or public trust, urging developers to use publicly available or duly authorised data without compromising critical electoral infrastructure. Meta’s Head of Public Policy for Anglophone West Africa, Sade Dada, said the increasing sophistication of AI-generated content was making it harder for people to distinguish authentic information from manipulated content.
“Elections are decided by voters. Voters make decisions based on what they believe, and what they believe depends on what they can trust,” Dada said. She identified cloned videos and synthetic voices as growing threats, noting that relatively simple tools now allow individuals to produce misleading content on a large scale.
However, Dada said AI could also help address the challenge through content verification, digital literacy initiatives and multilingual information services. She explained that Meta labels AI-generated content and requires advertisers to disclose the use of AI to significantly alter political advertisements, adding that the company’s technologies could help develop tools to identify manipulated images and videos.
Citing a local initiative, she said Meta had partnered with the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, the National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, and Publica AI to launch GovGuide Nigeria, an AI-powered chatbot that provides government information in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba. Dada said similar tools could enable voters to access reliable information on voter registration, polling units and electoral procedures in languages they understand.
The convener of the programme, Dr Toyosi Akerele-Ogunsiji, said the initiative aimed to translate discussions about AI into practical technological solutions to address electoral challenges ahead of the 2027 general election. She said the programme builds on Run-Am, an AI-powered application developed to detect misinformation and fact-check content during the 2023 elections. According to her, the initiative would feature a national hackathon, an AI Innovations Development Hub and a Community of Practice to nurture promising solutions beyond the competition.
Its focus areas include access to credible electoral information, election data analysis, inclusive and multilingual civic technology, cybersecurity and resilience, as well as election observation and citizen accountability. Akerele-Ogunsiji said participants must develop functional solutions rather than submit ideas or presentations alone. She added that applications were open to eligible Nigerians aged 18 and above. The application period opened on Thursday, October 22, and will close on November 12, 2026.
Participants may apply individually or in teams of up to four members. Russia's state-run oil giant Rosneft is facing mounting financial difficulties and the prospect of long-term damage as Ukraine expands its strike campaign against Russian oil refineries, Bloomberg reported on Oct. 22, citing expert analysts, insider sources, and documents reviewed by the outlet.
The news comes less than a week after the Ryazan Oil Refinery — one of Rosneft's biggest facilities — was reportedly forced to suspend operations at one of its main crude distillation units following a Ukrainian drone attack.
Officials at Rosneft have privately voiced concerns that even a few more months of Ukraine's continued attacks could lead to lasting damage for the company, according to Bloomberg.
Rosneft's 12 refineries account for approximately one third of Russia's total refining capacity. According to Bloomberg's analysis, five of 15 confirmed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries in September 2026 targeted Rosneft facilities that supply western Russia.
Documents reviewed by the outlet show that the Ryazan refinery has been shut down for more than half the time since it was hit by a Ukrainian drone blitz in May 2026. When it has been operational, the plant has run far below its actual capacity — a major blow to Russia's fourth-largest refinery, which supplies fuel to Moscow and the surrounding region.
Two other major Rosneft facilities have also suffered major disruptions over the past year. The Syzran refinery in Samara Oblast has been either completely offline or operating at below a third of its capacity for most of the past six months, data indicates.
The Syzran refinery has a processing capacity of approximately 9 million tons of crude oil per year and supplies fuel to the Russian Air Force and other military units. It also exports petroleum products via the Volga River and the Caspian Sea.
Rosneft's Tuapse refinery has been shut down since April, when Ukraine launched a sustained series of attacks against the key Black Sea export hub.

The success of Ukraine's attacks means Rosneft's profits continue to drop, despite the benefits the Iran war has channeled to the Russian oil industry.
Rosneft’s first-half net income in 2026 fell by almost 20%, to 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion), Bloomberg reports. Its ratio of net debt to earnings also rose by 1.8 times in the first half of the year, its highest level in over five years.
Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil assets increased dramatically in the past year, with the number of confirmed hits from January to October more than doubling in 2026 compared to 2025. Ukraine has carried out at least 114 attacks on refineries in Russia, an estimate Bloomberg based on public statements from both countries.
The constant pace of repairs has led to escalating costs that Rosneft officials say are unsustainable, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to Bloomberg. To cut costs, sources said, some refineries have deliberately stretched out repair work over several weeks.
Repairing and replacing damaged equipment is further complicated by international sanctions, which limit access to certain critical parts that would have previously been sourced from Western countries.
Rosneft said in a statement to Bloomberg that it is "taking appropriate measures to ensure the security and operation of our plants," and that "Not a single company petrol station has been closed, and consumers receive fuel in full at stable prices."
Russia has faced severe shortages of fuel in 2026, prompting sales restrictions and export bans — though U.S. President Donald Trump recently extended a lifeline to Moscow's struggling oil industry by announcing a controversial deal to buy Russian diesel.
While Ukraine briefly halted strikes on Russian oil refineries in October to honor Trump's proposed energy ceasefire, Kyiv soon resumed attacks when it became clear that Moscow had no intention of observing the truce.

Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.
He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.
"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.
"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

articles.title: Christa Pike's lawyer gives update on her condition after botched execution - Metro.co.uk
articles.summary: Christa Pike's lawyer gives update on her condition after botched execution  Metro.co.ukFrom death row to a botched execution and back: A timeline of Christa Pike’s case  CNNExecution staff warned IV site might have ‘blown’ during Christa Pike’s execution attempt  NBC NewsOne in three Americans back second execution attempt after failed one, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds  ReutersChrista Pike 'speaking in full sentences' as major health update given after botche...
articles.full_text:
Christa Pike is now speaking in full sentences and walking with far less help just three weeks after surviving her infamous failed execution attempt.
The 50-year-old was given two doses of pentobarbital as the state of Tennessee tried to carry out her death sentence on September 30. She somehow survived and was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious and needed a ventilator.
One of her lawyers told TMZ on Wednesday that her speech has improved considerably in recent days. Her mobility has also improved, allowing her to walk more independently as she continues her recovery in prison.
But medical staff are still monitoring her cognitive and psychological functioning. Her lawyer said it could take another month or longer to establish whether she has suffered any lasting damage or not.
Pike had been due to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. She was sentenced to death in 1996 for torturing and murdering her 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, the previous year.
Both were students at the Job Corps Centre in Knoxville. Pike was 18 when Slemmer was killed on January 12, 1995.
Prosecutors said Pike believed Slemmer was interested in her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Slemmer was attacked near the University of Tennessee’s agricultural campus, where she was beaten and stabbed before Pike struck her head with a large piece of asphalt.
More than three decades later, Pike was taken to the execution chamber at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Her lawyers say that the team carrying out the lethal injection repeatedly struggled to establish access to a vein.
According to a court filing from her legal team, at least seven needles were used during the attempt. One was bent at a 90-degree angle when it was removed, the filing said.
Her lawyers said she could be heard crying, whimpering and breathing loudly during the procedure. They reported that both her arms were swollen, burned and blistered when she arrived at hospital.
Pike’s legal team said they were subsequently told that she was totally brain dead and would soon be taken off life support. On October 6, however, she regained consciousness and began speaking.
Her lawyer Randy Spivey said that ‘to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking’.
According to Spivey, her first words were: ‘Where am I and who are you?’
He said she also asked about Slemmer’s family.
Pike’s lawyers reported that she suffered pneumonia, a blood clot in her arm and difficulty eating following the execution attempt.
Spivey described ‘extraordinary’ swelling in her hands, saying they ‘looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove’.
She was discharged from hospital on October 10 and transferred back to prison to continue receiving the necessary medical care.
Tennessee governor Bill Lee halted the state’s remaining executions for the year following the high profile botching of Pike’s execution.
Former US attorney Ed Stanton has been appointed to carry out an independent review into what happened.
The state’s prison chief, Frank Strada, also resigned in the aftermath. He said that stepping down while the review was conducted was ‘in the best interest of Tennesseans’.
Pike’s lawyers have urged Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, preventing another attempt to execute her. They argue she has ‘endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty’.

articles.title: North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South - The Guardian
articles.summary: North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South  The GuardianNorth Korea's Kim Yo Jong warns South Korea, says border loudspeakers to be ready within days  ReutersSouth Korea invites North for military talks over border  Al JazeeraNorth Korea plans to resume propaganda broadcasts along border with South Korea  Sky NewsNorth Korea threatens to "mercilessly eliminate" US-backed South Korean forces as its military ties raise co...
articles.full_text:
Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.
The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.
Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music and news criticising Pyongyang.
If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.
At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.
The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.
Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.
The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.
The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.
Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.
North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

First tanker loaded with Russian diesel is heading for New York after Moscow agreed to resume fuel exports to global markets under an arrangement reached between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump, according to LSEG shipping data.
The medium-sized vessel Agioi Fanendes took on 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22. It is expected to arrive in the United States on Nov. 7, Reuters reported.
The agreement reverses part of the restrictions that have kept Russian petroleum products out of Western markets since the war in Ukraine began in 2022.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, equivalent to 2.25 million barrels, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
The U.S. Treasury Department also issued a sanctions waiver allowing the sale, delivery and import of diesel fuel, including into the United States, through April 7, 2027.
Moscow subsequently began relaxing its self-imposed export restrictions, allowing shipments to resume despite earlier efforts to preserve domestic supplies.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has indicated that the country could restore monthly diesel exports to between 3 million tons and 3.5 million tons by the end of the year, approaching its usual export volume.
The deal has drawn criticism from Ukraine and some U.S. lawmakers, who argue that renewed purchases provide Moscow with revenue despite its ongoing war against Ukraine.
Russia has shifted much of its diesel trade toward markets outside Europe since the EU’s full embargo on Russian oil products took effect in February 2023. Türkiye, Brazil and several African countries have become important destinations for its fuel.
However, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have repeatedly disrupted fuel production, forcing Moscow to limit exports to protect domestic supplies.
The attacks have compounded the impact of refinery maintenance and other operational disruptions, leaving Russia with less diesel available for overseas buyers.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) reported that Russian refinery processing fell to 3.8 million barrels per day in June, its lowest level in more than 20 years and around 30% below the year-earlier level.
Diesel production was estimated to have declined by nearly 30% compared with 2025, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to preserve domestic supplies.
Russian diesel exports averaged around 345,000 barrels per day so far this year, down 41% from the previous year, according to shipping data cited by Reuters.
Before the restrictions, Russia was one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, with monthly shipments of diesel and gasoil substantially higher than recent levels.

Austria expelled four Russian diplomats over suspected Kremlin espionage, news magazine Profil reported on Oct. 23.
The expulsion order was authorized by Austrian Minister for European and International Affairs Beate Meinl-Reisinger, who pledged to systematically curb the Russian intelligence footprint and malign influence inside the country.
In mid-August, Austrian Ministry of Defense distributed an internal warning circular to active-duty military personnel and army reservists, alerting service members to aggressive outreach and recruitment attempts by suspected Russian clandestine operatives and ordering the immediate reporting of any such contacts.
The defense advisory included an intelligence dossier containing photographs and biographical files for 21 suspected individuals. While the underlying data was initially brought to light through an investigative leak published by independent Russian investigative outlet Proekt, Austrian counterintelligence services had placed these individuals under surveillance prior to the public disclosure.
Following intensive verification by security authorities, evidentiary dossiers compiled against three individuals on the watch list proved sufficiently conclusive to mandate their expulsion. In addition to the three embassy officials, a fourth Russian citizen accredited as a diplomat to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) — which maintains its permanent headquarters in Vienna — was ordered to depart Austrian territory.
Diplomatic Crackdowns and Regional Context
The Budapest expulsions on Sept. 8: The Austrian decision follows a significant diplomatic rupture in neighboring Hungary. On Sept. 8, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced the expulsion of ten Russian embassy officials from Budapest after Hungarian security services identified activities deemed "incompatible with diplomatic status" and in direct breach of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, framed as an emergency measure to protect Hungarian sovereignty.
Vienna as an espionage hub: Due to its host-nation status for major international bodies—including the United Nations, the IAEA, and the OSCE—coupled with Austria's historic constitutional neutrality, Vienna has long functioned as a primary European operational hub for Russian foreign intelligence (SVR) and military intelligence (GRU) clandestine networks.
Shifting security posture: The expulsions underscore a broader hardening of central European security postures against Russian hybrid warfare and intelligence operations, occurring as diplomatic negotiations and wartime tensions between Moscow and European capitals reach a boiling point in late October 2026.

articles.summary: Austria expels Russian diplomats suspected of espionage  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Austria expelled four Russian diplomats on Friday after accusing them of covertly working for Moscow’s intelligence agencies, in a sign of the neutral country’s toughening stance on Russia.
Officials said the individuals had been under surveillance by Austria’s domestic intelligence service for some time. Three were accredited diplomats at Russia’s embassy and the fourth worked at Russia’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) on military security and arms control.
Despite Austria’s small size, Vienna is one of Russia’s largest diplomatic hubs in Europe, with about 250 individuals registered to work in an official capacity as representatives of the Russian state.
Austria’s constitutional neutrality, weak laws on espionage and its establishment’s historically strong links with Russia have made the country a haven for Russian spies, at a time when the Kremlin’s agents have come under intense pressure elsewhere in Europe.
According to Austrian intelligence officials, up to a third of the officially accredited diplomats for Russia in the country are in fact working for Russian intelligence services. Most are tasked with carrying out duties such as running agent networks beyond Austria’s borders.
The Kremlin vowed it would take retaliatory measures. “The reaction will follow inevitably,” Russian deputy foreign minister Dmitry Lyubinsky said at a press briefing on Friday, according to newswire Interfax.
Successive Austrian governments have frustrated Kyiv and EU capitals with their reluctance to expel more Russian diplomats after President Vladimir Putin’s annexation of Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014 and the poisoning of Sergei Skripal in the UK in 2018.
The current coalition government, in power since 2025, has taken more steps, however, expelling seven Russian diplomats in total this year. This spring, Egisto Ott, a former counter-intelligence official, was convicted of working for Russian intelligence. Ott was a key figure in the network of the Austrian fugitive spy and mastermind of the Wirecard fraud, Jan Marsalek.
The other three diplomats were sent back to Moscow in May, in retaliation for what the Austrian government said was an unacceptable proliferation of antennas and digital equipment on the roofs of Russian diplomatic buildings in the capital intended for spying.
Those expulsions followed an FT investigation into the equipment in March.
Foreign minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said at the time that Austria had embarked on a “change of course” and would be taking “consistent” action against continuing Russian clandestine activity.

articles.title: What Israel’s Election Won't Change
articles.summary: The constraints and costs of the new security consensus.
articles.full_text:
When Israelis go to the polls on October 27, much of the world will be rooting for the defeat of the country’s longtime prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Under his nearly two decades of rule, Israel has become steadily more aggressive. It has abandoned any pretense of supporting a two-state solution; started constructing hundreds of new Jewish settlements in the West Bank; and, following Hamas’s cross-border attack on October 7, 2023, laid waste to the Gaza Strip, occupied parts of Lebanon and Syria, and launched war against Iran, its archnemesis. Meanwhile, its democratic institutions have faced endless attacks by Netanyahu and his allies, who have proposed laws that would, among other things, greatly curtail the power of Israel’s courts. Should he return to power for an unprecedented seventh term, many fret that the country will permanently transition into a rogue theocratic actor.
To many voters, this election thus marks a crucial turning point in Israeli domestic policy. The prime minister’s main political opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief Gadi Eisenkot, holds a more liberal worldview than his competitor. He supports an independent judiciary, a free press, and a professional civil service. Should he win, he will likely try to reverse Netanyahu’s efforts to curtail each institution’s independence.
But an Eisenkot victory is unlikely to change Israel’s foreign policy or approach to the Palestinians. Almost all of Israel’s Jewish political parties, Eisenkot’s included, are opposed to Palestinian statehood, not just Netanyahu’s Likud. They all believe that Israel’s brutal war on Gaza was morally just and practically necessary. And almost all of them think that Israel was right to attack Iran and to establish and create what its government and military call “security zones”—occupied territory—in Lebanon and Syria. In fact, the only real disagreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on matters of security is whether the latter made the right tactical decisions in each of these conflicts, such as when Netanyahu rejected a cease-fire in Gaza that would have freed Israeli hostages earlier.
That is not to say he will follow the same exact course. Eisenkot and Netanyahu differ in important ways on the barrage of West Bank settler attacks against helpless Palestinians, which are aimed at driving them out of their land. The prime minister, committed to his far-right allies, shrugs off the issue, whereas his competitor calls their behavior “Jewish terror.” Even if Eisenkot has little pity for the Palestinian victims, he realizes that the West Bank is on the verge of a bloody explosion and that Israel is at risk of even greater international opprobrium because of its reckless policy there. But overall, no matter what happens in the elections, Israel will continue to repress the Palestinians and strike its enemies. It will thus face diplomatic and economic costs, as the country’s frustrated partners begin cutting off aid and perhaps even enacting sanctions.
STYLE OVER SUBSTANCE
There are many issues at play in Israel’s election. Politicians, for example, have debated ultra-Orthodox exemptions from the draft, Netanyahu’s corruption charges, and what, if anything, the government should do about Jewish terrorism. But on the whole, the contest has been focused on who is to blame for failing to stop Hamas’s October 7 attack, which killed 1,200 Israelis and resulted in 251 more being taken hostage in one day. The opposition has argued that Netanyahu is responsible for the country’s worst-ever security failure, pointing out that he sustained Hamas with Qatari money, ignored intelligence warnings about Hamas plots, and then blocked an independent investigation into what happened. Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews to fighting in Gaza, has been particularly unsparing in his criticism, repeatedly hammering Netanyahu for refusing to take any accountability for the calamity. The prime minister and his supporters, for their part, have brushed off these missives. Instead, they have blamed October 7 on the military and security services. They have also promoted conspiracy theories that there is what Netanyahu’s cronies and supporters call “treason from within”—or that someone inside Israel helped facilitate Hamas’s brief invasion.
But despite this blame game, both sides agree on the tragedy’s primary lessons: that Israel is surrounded by diehard merciless enemies and that the Palestinians can never be trusted. This attitude is, in part, a raw expression of anti-Arab racism, which is more visible in Israel’s post–October 7 Jewish society. But it is also an electoral play. If the polling is correct, Eisenkot will need the support, however tacit, of Israel’s two Arab parties to put together a government. Netanyahu is thus trying to win over voters who, much as they hate him personally, cannot stand the idea of a government propped up by Palestinians.
This strategy is unlikely to work on liberal Israelis, who view this election as the last chance to save their homeland from sliding into dictatorship. Many Israelis who live abroad, including immigrants who left the country because of Netanyahu’s leadership, thus intend to come home and vote for his replacement. But these election day visitors and likeminded liberal voters are rallying to protect and preserve their way of life in a country that is becoming more religious and nationalistic. And even many of the anti-Netanyahu voters would be unhappy about partnering with the Arab parties to replace the current government. Few would bother to think about the two-state solution, viewing the idea as a relic from the overly optimistic 1990s. Eisenkot, the current leader of this electorate, has declared his personal opposition to a Palestinian state, as have Israel’s other centrist and conservative opposition figures. Only Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s sole left-wing Jewish party, supports what he calls “separation from the Palestinians” and a return to diplomacy—and even he lacks a plan for how to make that happen.
 Both sides agree: Israel is surrounded by merciless enemies and the Palestinians cannot be trusted.
In one sense, the country’s rejection of a two-state solution is not new. The last detailed negotiations over Palestinian statehood took place in early 2001. Most Jewish Israelis turned against the idea following the second intifada and Hamas’s 2007 takeover of Gaza. Netanyahu has railed against Palestinian sovereignty for his entire political career. (His brief ostensible endorsement of such a state, in 2009, was heavily conditioned and widely considered insincere.) And after October 7, opposition to the notion has become far more resolute. Before the attack, some major Jewish parties would still pay lip service to the notion of making peace with the Palestinians, and their politicians expressed tentative openness to a settlement. Now, they either reject it out of hand or simply dismiss the issue altogether.
Israeli officials have also become far more aggressive. The country may have turned against Palestinian independence years ago, but for most of the last two decades, it avoided full-scale wars and preserved the low-cost status quo. That restraint, even if disrupted by periodic rounds of fighting with Hamas, endeared Netanyahu to mainstream Israelis, who could pretend that the conflict was a thing of the past and all but forget about the Palestinians. Yet this attitude changed when Hamas crossed the border. Afterward, Israel adopted its current policy of destruction and occupation—which Netanyahu’s election campaign is bragging about, since it knows that bombing Iran and invading Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria have been extremely popular among the population at large. The prime minister’s main opponents all endorsed these tactics—criticizing him only for failing to achieve his pledge of “total victory.”
Netanyahu, in turn, blamed Eisenkot for being soft on Hamas when he served in the country’s war cabinet. Eisenkot then said that he had voted for a more aggressive invasion than what the prime minister ultimately undertook. Eisenkot later pledged to “end Hamas rule in Gaza within 18 months” if elected. This line is not necessarily as hawkish as Netanyahu’s posture, since it suggests a willingness to consider diplomatic means of removing the group from power. Eisenkot has also strongly criticized Netanyahu’s campaign pledge to overthrow the Iranian regime. Instead, he supports measures to take the enriched uranium out of Iran and to put its nuclear program under a verification regime. “You can’t overthrow a government from the air; it’s a delusion,” he said. But he nonetheless backed bombing the country to weaken its military and nuclear program, even if he disagreed with the ultimate end.
ANGER MANAGEMENT
The rest of the world, of course, does not share Israel’s view. Quite the contrary—in the wake of the destruction of Gaza, polls show that Israel’s international approval ratings have hit new lows. Politicians in every region are arguing that Israel is guilty of major human rights violations, with many claiming that the country has committed genocide. Even some of Israel’s friends are warning that the state has gone overboard. In July 2025, for example, U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer declared that although Israel “has a right to defend itself and end Hamas’s brutal rule,” the “reporting and images out of Gaza—depicting the devastating levels of hunger, starvation, suffering and death—are wholly unacceptable.”
Outside countries are also particularly furious about its settlement expansion in the West Bank, which cannot be justified as a reaction to October 7.
